title: Chances That Multiply
objective: After this level you can work out the chance of two independent things both happening, like rolling two sixes, by multiplying.
summary: For independent events, the chance of both is the product of their chances: two sixes is 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. Draw cards without putting them back and the draws are no longer independent.

cards.headline: What's the chance of rolling two sixes at once?
cards.body: You could list all 36 throws again and hunt for double 6. Or you could use a shortcut that works for any two unconnected chances, from dice to coins to cards. It takes one multiplication.

cards.headline: A fraction of a fraction
cards.body: The first die shows 6 one time in 6. Of those times, the second die also shows 6 just one time in 6. So double 6 happens a sixth of a sixth of the time: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. That matches Level 22's grid, where double 6 was exactly 1 of the 36 throws. The rule: when two events are independent, the chance of both is their chances multiplied.

cards.headline: It keeps multiplying
cards.body: The rule stretches to as many independent events as you like. Two heads in a row: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Three in a row: 1/8. Each extra flip halves the chance again, so ten heads in a row happens about once in 1,024 tries. Multiplying chances that are less than 1 always gives something smaller, which is why long runs are rare before they start.

cards.fact: Multiply only when one result leaves the other alone.
cards.context: Draw a card from a 52-card deck, put it back and shuffle: the second draw starts fresh, so the draws are independent. A heart, then another heart, is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Keep the first heart out, though, and the deck has changed: only 12 hearts are left among 51 cards. Without replacement, the first pick changes the chances for the second.

cards.headline: Chances: multiplied
learned: Ten heads in a row: 1 in 1,024

questions.prompt: Which rule gives the chance that two independent events both happen?

options.label: Add their chances
options.rationale: Adding would make "both" likelier than either alone.

options.label: Average their chances
options.rationale: Averaging would put "both" between the two chances; it must be smaller.

options.label: Take the larger chance
options.rationale: "Both" is less likely than either one on its own.

questions.explanation: For independent events, the chance that both happen is their chances multiplied together.

questions.prompt: How does keeping the first heart out of the deck change the chance that the next card is a heart?

options.label: It lowers it: 12 hearts are left among 51 cards
It raises it: fewer cards means better odds
options.rationale: Fewer cards, but fewer hearts too: 12 of 51 is below 1 in 4.

options.label: Nothing changes: it's still 1 in 4
options.rationale: 1 in 4 holds only if the heart goes back in the deck.

options.label: It makes a second heart impossible
options.rationale: Twelve hearts are still left to draw.

questions.explanation: Without replacement the deck changes: 12 hearts among 51 cards is a little less than 1 in 4, so the draws are dependent.

questions.prompt: Level 22 found double 6 in 1 of the 36 throws of two dice. Which calculation gives the same chance?

options.rationale: Adding gives 2/6, far too likely for two sixes at once.
A second die shows 6 one time in 6, not one time in 2.
6 × 6 counts the 36 throws, not the chance of one of them.

questions.explanation: Two independent chances of 1/6 multiply to 1/36: one throw in 36.
